title: Chest pain just as a sore throat was settling

source.citation: Jafri FN, Shulman J, Gómez-Márquez JC, Lazarus M, Ginsburg DM. Sore Throat, Fever, Septic Emboli, and Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Case of Lemierre Syndrome. Case Rep Emerg Med. 2018;2018:7373914.

presentation.hpi: Five days ago he woke up with a sore throat; his pediatrician's rapid group A streptococcal swab was negative. Over the next three days he developed nausea, vomiting, intermittent fevers, sweats and chills, and on a second visit his pediatrician started oseltamivir for presumed influenza. The sore throat and chills improved last night, but he then developed severe suprasternal chest discomfort and pleuritic chest pain.
meds: Oseltamivir, started by his pediatrician for presumed influenza
presentation.social: Has never used alcohol or illicit drugs.

exam: Drowsy but oriented to person, place and time
Shortly after the initial evaluation: fever of 103 °F (39.4 °C)
Moist mucous membranes; no throat exudates
No carotid bruits; no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy
Lungs clear on auscultation; no heart murmur
No cyanosis or mottling of the skin

imaging.finding: Bibasilar patchy infiltrates, right greater than left, with additional scattered nodular opacities
Marked progression of bilateral pulmonary infiltrates

imaging.modality: CT neck and chest with IV contrast (after blood cultures turned positive)
imaging.finding: Complete occlusion of the right internal jugular vein with surrounding inflammatory change (thrombophlebitis), a 0.6 cm right peritonsillar abscess, and multiple cavitary and non-cavitary pulmonary nodules consistent with septic emboli

diagnosis.primary: Lemierre syndrome (Fusobacterium necrophorum bacteremia with right internal jugular vein septic thrombophlebitis, a small peritonsillar abscess and septic pulmonary emboli) complicated by sepsis with hypotension and ARDS
differentials: Right-sided infective endocarditis with septic emboli

management: Blood cultures, then levofloxacin and clindamycin for presumed bilateral community-acquired pneumonia
ICU admission for hypotension, bandemia and lactic acidosis
Within 12 h, ARDS with severe hypoxemia: intubation and pressure-control ventilation with PEEP up to 20 cm H2O and neuromuscular blockade
Transferred to a tertiary center for possible ECMO, which was not needed
Contrast CT of the neck and chest once blood cultures grew F. necrophorum; antibiotics continued as meropenem and linezolid
outcome: Continued on meropenem and linezolid and liberated from mechanical ventilation over the following days, without needing ECMO.
teachingPoints: Lemierre syndrome typically strikes healthy adolescents and young adults: pharyngitis, then (often after apparent improvement) rigors, sepsis and septic emboli, usually to the lungs, within about a week.
A negative rapid streptococcal test does not exclude Fusobacterium necrophorum pharyngitis.
Sepsis with thrombocytopenia, raised bilirubin and multiple nodular or cavitating lung lesions after a recent sore throat should prompt contrast CT of the neck.

Treat with antibiotics that reliably cover anaerobes (piperacillin–tazobactam, a carbapenem, or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole) and drain any collection; the role of anticoagulation remains unsettled.
Septic pulmonary emboli can progress to ARDS within hours.

questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.extra: WBC 17 × 10³/µL with 28% bands, platelets 50 × 10³/µL, total bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL, lactic acid 3.1 mmol/L, troponin negative. Chest radiograph: no acute abnormality. Non-contrast CT chest: bibasilar patchy infiltrates with scattered nodular opacities.
options: Lemierre syndrome with septic pulmonary emboli
Acute pulmonary embolism with lung infarction
questions.explanation: A young adult whose pharyngitis seemed to settle, then sepsis with hypotension, thrombocytopenia, raised bilirubin and scattered nodular lung opacities, should be assumed to have Lemierre syndrome until a contrast neck CT says otherwise. Nodules in this setting suggest septic emboli rather than simple pneumonia, and a negative rapid strep test does not exclude Fusobacterium.

questions.q: Which investigation will best confirm the diagnosis?
options: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest
questions.explanation: Contrast CT of the neck shows internal jugular thrombophlebitis and any peritonsillar or parapharyngeal collection, and extending it to the chest shows the septic emboli. Ultrasound can show a jugular thrombus but sees poorly beneath the clavicle and mandible; blood cultures usually grow F. necrophorum, but only after days.

questions.q: Which empiric antibiotic regimen is most appropriate once this diagnosis is suspected?
questions.explanation: Fusobacterium necrophorum is an obligate anaerobe, intrinsically resistant to macrolides and occasionally beta-lactamase producing, so treatment needs reliable anaerobic cover: piperacillin–tazobactam, a carbapenem, or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, usually for several weeks with drainage of collections. Vancomycin and aztreonam have no useful activity against it.

evidence.quote: An eighteen-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with fever and severe chest pain.
His symptoms developed five days earlier when he woke up with a sore throat.
He was seen by his pediatrician who performed a negative Rapid Group-A Streptococcus swab.
Over the following three days, he developed nausea, vomiting, intermittent fevers, sweats, and chills.
He went back to his pediatrician who this time started him empirically on oseltamivir phosphate for presumed influenza.
His symptoms of sore throat and chills improved the night prior to admission, but then he developed severe suprasternal chest discomfort and pleuritic chest pain.
He had never used alcohol or illicit drugs.
He was hypotensive with a blood pressure of 88/46 mmHg and a heart rate of 127 beats per minute. His initial saturation was 99% on room air.
the patient was initially afebrile, but shortly after his initial evaluation he developed a fever of 103 degrees Fahrenheit
On examination, he was noted to be drowsy but oriented to person, place, and time.
He had moist mucous membranes and no throat exudates.
He had no carotid bruits or cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy.
His pulmonary auscultation was normal, and his heart exam had no murmurs.
He had no cyanosis or mottling of skin.
Labs were notable for white count of 17 thousand per mL with 28% bands, total bilirubin of 2.4 mg/dL, platelet count of 50 thousand per mL
lactic acid of 3.1 mg/dL, and a negative troponin
Two days later, patient had two blood cultures which grew Fusobacterium necrophorum.
A plain chest X-ray had no acute abnormalities
There are bibasilar patchy infiltrates, right greater than left (black arrows). There are additional scattered nodular opacities
Within 12 hours, he had a rapid and sharp clinical decline with worsening and severe hypoxemia and marked progression of his bilateral pulmonary infiltrates readily evidenced on CXR.
demonstrating a right internal jugular thrombophlebitis, a 0.6 cm right peritonsillar abscess, and multiple pulmonary cavitary infiltrates consistent with septic emboli
There is complete occlusion of the right internal jugular vein (black arrow).
A small amount of hypodense fluid surrounding the occluded right internal jugular vein reflects inflammatory changes.
Multiple nodules were visualized in the imaged portion of the chest, including cavitary (black arrow) and noncavitary nodules
He was diagnosed with Lemierre's syndrome.
After blood cultures were drawn and with a presumed diagnosis of bilateral community acquired pneumonia, Levofloxacin, and Clindamycin were initiated.
Because of hypotension, bandemia, and lactic acidosis, he was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit for further monitoring.
He required mechanical ventilation and was diagnosed with Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS).
Pressure control ventilation with positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) up to 20 cm H20 and paralytics were needed to maintain adequate oxygenation and saturation.
He was subsequently transferred to a tertiary care center for further management and possible Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO) which in the end he did not require.
Upon notification of the positive blood cultures, he had a CT scan of his neck with intravenous contrast
Over the course of the next few days, he continued treatment with Meropenem and Linezolid and was liberated from mechanical ventilation.
